articles.title: Rainscreen walls, sheathing membrane (WRB) and the capillary break
articles.summary: Wall cladding is the first plane of protection; behind it a drained and vented gap and the sheathing membrane (water-resistive barrier, WRB) form the second plane. BCBC defines the capillary break options, such as a drained, vented air space at least 9.5 mm deep behind the cladding (usually 19 mm strapping). In most of coastal BC a capillary break is required based on climate; inland, check the location.
articles.why: Coastal BC learned this the hard way in the 1990s leaky-condo crisis. A rainscreen lets water that gets past the siding drain out and the wall dry.
steps: Install the sheathing membrane shingle-fashion (upper over lower), lapped at least 100 mm horizontally and 150 mm at vertical joints, or as the maker specifies.
Integrate it with window and door flashings (see the window installation article).
Fasten vertical strapping (typically 19 x 64 mm) over the studs to create the cavity.
Install insect screen at the bottom and top of the cavity, leaving it open to drain and vent.
Fasten cladding through the strapping into the framing.

tolerances.item: Drained and vented air space (one capillary-break option)
tolerances.value: at least 9.5 mm deep, full height and width
required behind cladding, installed per the code
upper over lower, at least about 100 mm, or as the maker specifies

mistakes: Reverse laps (lower over upper) that funnel water behind the WRB.
Blocking the bottom of the cavity with trim or sealant.
Tears from wind or staples left unrepaired.
checkpoints: Many BC municipalities inspect the WRB and window flashings before cladding.

articles.title: Window installation and the flashing sequence
articles.summary: Windows are installed so water that gets behind the frame drains out. The usual BC rainscreen sequence is - sill membrane (sloped, turned up at the back and ends), jambs, set the window in a continuous bead at the jambs and head (but not the sill), head flashing over the nailing flange, then the head membrane lapped over that. An interior air seal around the frame completes it.
articles.why: Windows are the most common leak location in houses. The order of laps decides whether water drains out or in.
steps: Check the rough opening - size, square, level sill; slope the sill to the outside if detailed.
Install sill membrane (self-adhered), with back dam and end dams, turned up the jambs.
Install jamb membranes lapped over the sill membrane.
Set the window plumb, level and square on shims; fasten per the maker. Leave the sill flange unsealed so it drains.
Install the head flashing, then lap the WRB or a head membrane over it.
Seal the interior gap with low-expansion foam or backer rod and sealant for air tightness.

tolerances.value: flashing per 9.27.3.7/9.27.3.8 and sealants per 9.27.4
per the window maker's instructions and installation standard
continuous between frame and rough opening

mistakes: Sealing the bottom flange so water cannot get out.
Head membrane tucked under the head flashing.
High-expansion foam bowing the frame.
checkpoints: Window and membrane inspection before cladding (where the municipality inspects it).

articles.title: Flashing at cladding junctions, decks and penetrations
articles.summary: Flashing directs water out of the wall at every horizontal break - between different claddings, at offsets, over windows and doors, at deck ledgers and roof-wall junctions. It is required at every horizontal junction between cladding elements unless the upper cladding overlaps the lower by at least 25 mm or another exception applies. Flashing must slope out and lap over the material below.
articles.why: Water follows gravity and laps. Any horizontal ledge without flashing becomes a leak.
steps: Identify every horizontal junction on the elevations.
Install flashing sloped outward with a drip edge, its back leg lapped under the WRB above.
At deck ledgers, use a membrane behind the ledger and a flashing over it.
At roof-to-wall junctions, step flashing plus a kick-out at the bottom.

tolerances.value: at horizontal cladding junctions, offsets and substrate changes (exceptions apply)
per the code material requirements

mistakes: Missing kick-out flashing where a roof edge meets a wall.
Flashing back leg on top of the WRB.

articles.title: Cladding attachment and clearances
articles.summary: Siding (fibre-cement, vinyl, wood, metal, stucco) is fastened to framing or furring with corrosion-resistant fasteners of the size and spacing the code and the maker require. Clearances to grade, roofs and decks keep the cladding dry, and expansion gaps let it move.

tolerances.value: per the code for the cladding type
per the code and the maker
as the cladding maker requires (often 150 mm to grade, 50 mm to roofs)

mistakes: Fibre-cement cut ends left unsealed or touching the roof.
Vinyl siding nailed tight so it cannot expand.

articles.title: Air barrier - continuity is everything
articles.summary: The air barrier system stops air leaking through the envelope. It can be on the inside (sealed polyethylene or airtight drywall), the outside (taped sheathing or a sealed membrane), or both, but it must be continuous across joints, between assemblies and around penetrations. BCBC lists the problem details - rim joists, wall-to-ceiling junctions, interior walls meeting exterior walls, windows, and service penetrations.
articles.why: Air leakage carries moisture into walls and attics (condensation) and is often the biggest energy loss. Step Code houses are blower-door tested, so gaps show up as a failed number.
steps: Decide where the air barrier is on every assembly and how it connects at transitions (draw it as one continuous line on the section).
Seal the sill plate to the foundation and the rim joist.
Lap and seal sheet joints, or lap 100 mm and clamp between framing and a rigid material.
Carry the air barrier across interior wall intersections and attic hatches; seal top plates.
Seal around windows, doors, ducts, pipes and wires (see penetrations).
Do a mid-construction blower door test before drywall if the house has a target.

tolerances.value: sealed, or lapped at least 100 mm and clamped
air barrier extended across or the space blocked
across joints, between assemblies, around penetrations

mistakes: Interior partitions framed before the ceiling poly is run past the top plate.
Unsealed electrical boxes and plumbing stacks.
Attic hatch with no weatherstrip.
checkpoints: Insulation and vapour/air barrier inspection before drywall.
Mid-construction blower door test.

articles.title: Vapour barrier (vapour retarder) - warm side, and where low-permeance layers go
articles.summary: A vapour barrier on the warm (inside) side of the insulation limits water vapour diffusing into the cold part of the wall. Polyethylene often serves as both air and vapour barrier. Low-permeance materials (foam board, some membranes) on the cold side are only allowed when enough insulation is outboard of them to keep their inner face warm - the code gives the ratio by climate.
articles.why: Vapour trapped between two low-perm layers condenses and rots sheathing.

tolerances.value: required on the warm side of insulated assemblies
joints lapped, around openings sealed where it is also the air barrier

tolerances.item: Low-permeance material on the cold side
tolerances.value: only with the required outboard thermal resistance ratio

mistakes: Poly on both sides of the wall (a "double vapour barrier").
Exterior foam too thin for the climate, putting the sheathing below dew point.

articles.title: Insulation installation and effective R-value
articles.summary: Insulation must fill the cavity without gaps, voids or compression and be in full contact with the air barrier side. The code measures effective thermal resistance (RSI) of the whole assembly including framing, so studs, headers and corners reduce the number. Step Code houses often add exterior insulation or use advanced framing to cut thermal bridging.
articles.why: A 5% void can cost far more than 5% of the insulation's value; compressed batts lose R-value.
steps: Cut batts to fit snugly around boxes, pipes and wires (split the batt around wires).
Fill headers, corners and rim joists.
Install baffles at the eaves before attic insulation so vents stay open.
Mark attic insulation depth gauges for blown-in insulation.

tolerances.value: in full contact, no voids or compression, protected from air movement
per the 9.36 tables for the climate zone or energy model
across assembly junctions

mistakes: Batts stuffed behind wires and pipes, leaving gaps at the front.
No insulation in headers or behind tubs on exterior walls.
checkpoints: Insulation inspection before drywall.

articles.title: Attic and roof space venting
articles.summary: A vented attic needs unobstructed vent area of at least 1/300 of the insulated ceiling area (1/150 for low slopes under 1 in 6 or joist-type roofs), split so at least 25% is at the top and 25% at the bottom, spread evenly on opposite sides. Baffles keep insulation from blocking soffit vents.
articles.why: Venting removes moisture that gets into the attic; it does not fix air leaks from the house below - seal those first.

tolerances.value: at least 1/300 of insulated ceiling area

tolerances.item: Vent area, slope under 1 in 6 or roof joists
tolerances.value: at least 1/150
at least 25% high and 25% low, both sides

tolerances.item: Clearance between insulation and roof sheathing
tolerances.value: per the code

Soffit vents covered by insulation.

articles.title: Sealing service penetrations (electrical, plumbing, ducts)
articles.summary: Every wire, pipe, duct and box that passes through the air barrier is a leak unless it is sealed. Use airtight electrical boxes or box gaskets on exterior walls and ceilings, rubber gaskets or tape on pipes and ducts, and fire-rated sealant where the penetration also passes a fire separation or fire block.
articles.why: Penetrations made by trades after the framing is done are the main cause of failed blower door tests.
steps: Plan penetrations through the top plates and exterior walls and keep them few.
Use airtight boxes on exterior walls and insulated ceilings.
Seal pipe and duct penetrations with gaskets, tape or sealant compatible with the air barrier.
Use firestop products where fire blocks or separations are penetrated.

tolerances.value: sealed
tightly fitted or sealed so the fire block still works

mistakes: Holes drilled oversize "for the next guy".
Spray foam used where a fire-rated sealant is required.

articles.title: Roof underlay and eave protection
articles.summary: Eave protection (usually a self-adhered modified-bitumen membrane) runs up from the roof edge to at least 300 mm inside the inner face of the exterior wall to stop ice-dam leaks. The code waives it in some cases - including regions with 3 500 or fewer degree-days, which covers much of coastal BC - but most shingle makers' warranties and good practice still call for it at eaves and in valleys.
articles.why: Ice dams push melt water up under shingles. Where the code does not require eave protection, the shingle warranty often still does.
steps: Install drip edge at the eave, membrane over it, then drip edge at the rakes over the underlay.
Run eave protection from the edge to 300 mm inside the wall line (often two courses).
Line valleys with membrane.
Lay synthetic underlay over the rest of the deck, lapped as the maker specifies.

tolerances.value: from the edge to at least 300 mm inside the inner face of the wall
e.g. 3 500 or fewer degree-days, slopes 1 in 1.5 or steeper, big overhangs
per the shingle maker's instructions for the slope

mistakes: Membrane stopped at the wall line instead of 300 mm inside it.
Drip edge on top of the membrane at the eave in the wrong order.

articles.title: Asphalt shingles - slope, exposure and nailing
articles.summary: Each roof covering has a minimum slope; asphalt shingles on low slopes need extra underlay. Shingles are applied with a starter strip, the right head lap and exposure, and fastened with the number and placement of nails printed on the bundle - high nailing is the most common cause of blow-offs.
steps: Check the roof slope against the code table and the shingle instructions.
Install a starter strip at eaves and rakes.
Snap lines for exposure; nail in the nail line with 4 or 6 nails as required for the wind zone.
Finish hips and ridges with cap shingles and vents as designed.

tolerances.value: per the code table
number, length and placement per the code and bundle
as printed on the bundle

mistakes: Nails above the nail line.
Over-driven nails cutting the mat.

articles.title: Roof flashing - valleys, step flashing, chimneys and saddles
articles.summary: Flashing is required wherever a roof meets a wall, chimney or another roof plane. Valleys are open (metal) or closed (woven or cut) over a membrane; walls get step flashing woven with each shingle course and counter flashing; chimneys wider than a set size get a saddle (cricket) on the upslope side.

per the code options
step and counter flashing per the code
where required by chimney width

mistakes: Continuous L-flashing instead of step flashing at a sidewall.
No kick-out at the bottom of a roof-wall junction.

articles.title: Fire blocking in concealed spaces
articles.summary: Fire blocks stop fire and smoke spreading through hidden spaces. Vertical spaces in walls must be blocked off from each other and from horizontal spaces (floors, ceilings, attics), and wall cavities blocked at each floor level, with blocks no more than 20 m apart horizontally and 3 m vertically. Accepted materials include 38 mm lumber, two layers of 19 mm lumber, 12.7 mm gypsum board, 12.5 mm plywood or OSB with supported joints, or 0.38 mm sheet steel. Walls fully filled with insulation are exempt from some of these rules.
articles.why: Platform framing makes most fire blocks automatically (plates at each floor). The gaps are at soffits, dropped ceilings, stairs, chases, tubs, and furred-out walls.
steps: Check every vertical chase, soffit, dropped ceiling and stair against the rules.
Block furred spaces at floor and ceiling levels.
Block at the top and bottom of stair runs where required.
Seal penetrations through fire blocks so they still work.

tolerances.value: at each floor level; max 20 m horizontal and 3 m vertical between blocks
38 mm lumber, 2 x 19 mm lumber, 12.7 mm gypsum, 12.5 mm plywood/OSB, 0.38 mm steel (or tested)

mistakes: Chase around a flue or stack left open floor to attic.
Furred basement walls with no blocking at the top.

checkpoints: Framing inspection - chases, soffits and furring.

articles.title: Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms
articles.summary: Every dwelling needs smoke alarms on every storey including the basement, in every bedroom, and in the hallway (or between bedrooms and the rest of the storey), installed on or near the ceiling, permanently wired and interconnected so one sets them all off. Carbon monoxide alarms are required where the house has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage.

all alarms in a dwelling interconnected
permanently connected, with battery backup where required
where a fuel-burning appliance or storage garage serves the house

mistakes: Missing alarm in a basement bedroom.
Alarm box beside a bathroom door (nuisance alarms) or in the dead-air corner.

articles.title: Attached garages - gas-tight separation
articles.summary: An attached garage must be separated from the house by a barrier that keeps exhaust gases out - sealed drywall or another air barrier on the common walls and ceiling, a tight-fitting self-closing door, and no ducts or openings that connect the garage air to the house. Houses with an attached garage also need CO alarms.

tolerances.value: gas-tight per the code

articles.title: BC Energy Step Code for houses
articles.summary: The BC Energy Step Code is the performance path in BCBC 9.36.6. A house is modelled by an Energy Advisor and must meet the step's targets - percent heat-loss reduction and percent energy improvement over a reference house, plus an airtightness test. Province-wide the minimum is now Step 3 for Part 9 homes, and local governments can require higher steps by bylaw. The Zero Carbon Step Code (Section 9.37) separately limits greenhouse gas emissions.
articles.why: The step sets the envelope, windows, airtightness and mechanical systems the framing has to deliver - for example 2x6 walls, exterior insulation, or fewer thermal bridges.
steps: Check the step required by the municipality on the permit date.
Engage a registered Energy Advisor at design; get the pre-construction model and compliance report.
Build to the modelled specs (insulation, windows, airtightness, HRV, heat pump).
Mid-construction blower door test (recommended); final test and as-built report for occupancy.

tolerances.value: targets of the applicable step in Table 9.36.6.3.-G
per the code modelling rules
Step 3 province-wide; higher where the local bylaw requires

mistakes: Changing windows or wall assemblies after the model without re-modelling.
Leaving airtightness to the end.

articles.title: Airtightness testing (blower door)
articles.summary: Step Code houses are blower-door tested to CAN/CGSB-149.10 under BCBC 9.36.7, which also defines the metrics - air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50) and the newer normalized leakage area (NLA10) and normalized leakage rate (NLR50). A mid-construction test, after the air barrier is complete but before drywall, is the time to find and fix leaks.
steps: Schedule a mid-construction test once windows, doors, the air barrier and penetrations are done.
During the test, walk the house with smoke or a thermal camera and seal leaks.
Final test at completion for the as-built Energy Advisor report.

determined per the code metrics (ACH50, NLA10, NLR50)

mistakes: First test at final, when leaks are behind drywall.

articles.title: Climate zones and degree-days in BC
articles.summary: Section 9.36 groups locations into climate zones by heating degree-days (HDD, Celsius) - Zone 4 under 3 000, Zone 5 3 000-3 999, Zone 6 4 000-4 999, Zone 7A 5 000-5 999, Zone 7B 6 000-6 999 and Zone 8 7 000 and over. Most of the Lower Mainland and southern Vancouver Island is Zone 4; the Interior is mostly Zones 5 to 7A; the north is 7A to 8. Degree-days also decide whether eave protection is required (over 3 500).

articles.title: Zero Carbon Step Code
articles.summary: The Zero Carbon Step Code (BCBC Section 9.37) sets greenhouse-gas emission levels for new houses, from measure-only up to zero-carbon performance. Local governments choose the level by bylaw; in practice the higher levels mean electric heat pumps and electric hot water instead of gas.

articles.title: Finished flooring and underlay
articles.summary: Finished flooring goes over a subfloor and, where the flooring type requires, a panel-type underlay with offset joints and the specified fastening. articles.title: Bedroom egress windows
articles.summary: Unless the suite is sprinklered, every bedroom needs at least one window or exterior door that opens from inside without tools, giving a clear opening of at least 0.35 m2 with no dimension under 380 mm. Where it opens into a window well, at least 760 mm of clear space is needed in front of the window. The rough opening and header are set in framing, so egress is checked on the plan.

articles.title: Fall protection on residential sites
articles.summary: WorkSafeBC requires a fall protection system where a worker could fall 3 m (10 ft) or more, or from a lower height where the fall could cause serious injury (onto rebar, into an excavation). On houses this means guardrails on floor edges and openings, covers on holes, and travel restraint or fall arrest on roofs and while setting trusses or joists. A written fall protection plan is needed where fall arrest is used above 7.5 m or where guardrails are not practicable.
steps: Install guardrails on decks, stair openings and window openings as the floor is built.
Cover and mark floor openings.
Plan anchor points for roof work before sheathing is complete.

tolerances.value: 3 m, or less where the risk is unusual

articles.title: Excavation safety - sloping, shoring and spoil
articles.summary: Excavations deeper than 1.2 m (4 ft) that workers enter must be sloped, benched or shored as WorkSafeBC requires, or as designed by an engineer, unless an engineer says it is safe. Spoil and equipment are kept back from the edge, and utilities are located first.

articles.title: Saws, nailers and the cutting machine
articles.summary: Power tool injuries on framing sites come mostly from circular saws, mitre saws and nailers. Guards must stay in place, sequential-trip (single-shot) nailers reduce double-fire and bump injuries, and eye and hearing protection are standard. The Acucut by HASWORKS HOMES cutting cell keeps people out of the blade zone with a light curtain and interlocked guards.

articles.title: Silica dust from concrete and fibre-cement
articles.summary: Cutting, grinding or drilling concrete, masonry and fibre-cement siding releases respirable crystalline silica, which causes silicosis and lung cancer. WorkSafeBC requires an exposure control plan, and wet cutting or tool-mounted dust extraction with respirators where needed.

articles.title: Building permits, Schedules and who signs what
articles.summary: In BC, building permits are issued by the local government (the city, district or regional district) under the BC Building Code, or the Vancouver Building By-law in Vancouver. Part 9 houses are usually designed without an architect, but structural items outside Part 9 need an engineer who provides letters of assurance (Schedules B and C-B). Electrical and gas permits come from Technical Safety BC or the city where delegated. New homes need a licensed residential builder and home warranty insurance.
steps: Confirm which code applies (BCBC or VBBL) and the Step Code and Zero Carbon levels.
Submit drawings, energy model, site survey and any engineer's Schedules.
Display the permit on site and keep approved drawings available for the inspector.

articles.title: Typical BC inspection sequence for a new house
articles.summary: Each municipality sets its own inspection list, but a typical BC house goes through - footing forms (before pour), foundation and perimeter drain with dampproofing (before backfill), under-slab plumbing and radon/poly (before the slab), framing with sheathing and WRB (after roof, windows and rough-ins), plumbing, electrical and gas rough-ins, a mid-construction blower door test for Step Code, insulation and vapour/air barrier (before drywall), and final/occupancy with the Energy Advisor's as-built report and any Schedules. The HASWORKS HOMES build order and photo record are organised around these hold points.
articles.why: Each inspection is a hold point - work covered before it passes has to be opened up.
steps: Footing - forms, rebar, bearing soil and depth.
Foundation and drain tile - walls, dampproofing, drains, before backfill.
Under-slab - plumbing test, poly and radon pipe, before pour.
Framing - structure, fire blocking, bracing, WRB and windows; after plumbing, electrical, gas and HVAC rough-ins pass.
Insulation and air/vapour barrier - before drywall; mid-construction blower door where required.
Final - life safety, guards, smoke and CO alarms, grading, Energy Advisor report, Schedules, warranty enrolment.

tolerances.value: set by the local government

mistakes: Calling for framing before the trades' rough-ins pass.
Insulating before the electrical rough-in inspection.

citations.note: typical sequence compiled from BC municipal inspection checklists; varies by municipality

articles.title: Home warranty (2-5-10) and builder licensing in BC
articles.summary: Under the Homeowner Protection Act, new homes in BC must be built by a licensed residential builder (or an owner-builder with authorization) and covered by third-party home warranty insurance - generally 2 years on materials, labour and major systems, 5 years on the building envelope (including water penetration), and 10 years on structural defects. The HASWORKS HOMES per-piece photo record and inspection log are useful evidence for warranty claims.

tolerances.value: 2-5-10 minimum coverage under the Homeowner Protection Act regulations

citations.note: BC Housing Licensing and Consumer Services - home warranty and licensing

articles.title: Platform framing sequence - why pieces go in this order
articles.summary: Platform framing builds one storey at a time. The floor deck is finished first, walls are framed flat on it and stood up, then the next floor or the roof bears on the capped walls. The HASWORKS HOMES build order follows this load path, so every piece is installed onto something that already carries it.
articles.why: Installing out of order means pieces are toe-nailed into place later, cap plates cannot lap, and bracing goes into walls that are not yet plumb. It also creates work at height without a deck to stand on.
steps: Sills, beams and posts on the foundation, then rim joists, then floor joists and blocking.
Subfloor glued and nailed. This is the platform for the walls.
Exterior walls first (they square and stiffen the deck), then interior partitions between them.
Within a wall - plates laid out, studs, opening members (kings, jacks, headers, sills, cripples), bracing, then the lapped cap plate once intersecting walls stand.
Next floor or ceiling joists tie the wall tops before rafters push outward on them.
Ridge and roof beams, rafters, then collar ties or rafter ties.
Stairs once the storey is closed in and the openings are framed.

tolerances.item: Walls plumb before bracing and sheathing
tolerances.value: within about 3 mm over a 2.4 m stud (1/8 in in 8 ft)
diagonals equal within about 6 mm on a typical house deck

mistakes: Standing partitions before exterior walls, so the deck is never squared to the long walls.
Nailing the cap plate on before the intersecting wall is in, so it cannot lap.
Rafters cut and set before ceiling joists or a structural ridge hold the wall tops - the walls spread.
checkpoints: Deck square and level before wall layout.
Every wall braced or sheathed before the next floor loads it.
safety: Plan fall protection before joist work on the second floor (WorkSafeBC Part 11 applies from 3 m).

articles.title: Framing lumber - sizes, grades, moisture and crown
articles.summary: Canadian dimension lumber is sold by nominal size (2x4, 2x6) but is smaller when dressed - 38 x 89 mm for a 2x4, 38 x 140 for a 2x6, 38 x 184 for a 2x8, 38 x 235 for a 2x10, 38 x 286 for a 2x12. Structural framing must be grade-stamped (S-P-F No.2 or better is typical for studs and joists), and should be dry (S-Dry, 19% moisture or less) to limit shrinkage.
articles.why: The span tables, nailing rules and the cut list all assume a known species group, grade and dressed size. Wet lumber shrinks across the grain as it dries, which opens drywall joints, pops nails and drops floors at bearing walls.
steps: Check the grade stamp - species group, grade, mill, and S-Dry or KD-HT.
Sight each joist, rafter and header and mark the crown (the high edge); install crown up.
Keep lumber stacked off the ground on stickers and covered, with air flow.
Use pressure-treated lumber where wood touches concrete near grade or is within 150 mm of the ground, per the decay rules.

tolerances.item: Moisture content at time of installation
tolerances.value: 19% or less recommended (S-Dry)

mistakes: Mixing crown-up and crown-down joists, giving a wavy floor.
Using untreated wood in contact with concrete at grade.
Using ungraded lumber for structural members.
checkpoints: Grade stamps visible on structural members.
Treated wood or a moisture barrier where wood meets concrete.

citations.note: Chapter 4 moisture relations, Chapter 13 drying and dimensional change

articles.title: Beams, posts and bearing
articles.summary: A beam (girder) carries floor joists over a long span and delivers load to posts and the foundation. Built-up beams are made of 38 mm members on edge nailed together, with butt joints only over supports. Beams need even, level bearing of at least 89 mm at the ends, and posts must be anchored top and bottom.
articles.why: Beams and posts concentrate load. Short bearing, joints mid-span or an unanchored post are classic causes of sagging floors and failed inspections.
steps: Confirm beam size and post spacing from the plans or span tables; engineered beams (LVL, glulam) follow the supplier's design.
Set posts on footings with a moisture break; anchor posts top and bottom.
Assemble built-up beams with joints over posts and nail per the nailing schedule.
Shim to full, even bearing - no point bearing on a single shim.

tolerances.value: 89 mm minimum
38 mm or thicker, on edge, butt joints over supports (with limited exceptions)

mistakes: Butt joints between posts.
Steel shims or hardwood wedges giving point bearing.
Post not anchored to the beam (uplift and lateral movement).
checkpoints: Bearing length and post anchorage before the subfloor covers it.

citations.note: spans for joists, rafters and beams (span tables - not reproduced)

articles.title: Rim joists (header joists) and floor layout
articles.summary: The rim joist (also called header joist or band joist) closes the ends of the floor joists around the perimeter. It carries the joist layout marks, holds joists upright, transfers wall loads to the sill and is a key air-sealing location.
articles.why: Getting the rims straight, flush with the foundation and marked accurately sets the layout for every joist and every wall above.
steps: Snap the outside line on the sill so the rim is flush with the foundation face (or set back for exterior insulation as designed).
Mark joist layout on the rim, typically 400 mm (16 in) on centre, starting from the same end as the wall layout above so loads stack.
Toe-nail the rim to the sill per the nailing schedule.
Air-seal the rim to the sill and subfloor (sealant or tape) and insulate the rim space later.

tolerances.value: 400 mm (16 in) typical; 300 or 600 where designed

mistakes: Starting layout from opposite ends on different floors, so studs and joists do not stack.
Leaving the rim unsealed - a major air leak in older houses.
checkpoints: Rim flush and straight; layout marks match the plans.

citations.note: air barrier details at rim joists

articles.title: Floor joists - spans, bearing and layout
articles.summary: Floor joists span between foundation walls, beams and bearing walls. Their size comes from the span tables (or the I-joist maker's tables) for the species, grade, spacing and load. Each joist needs at least 38 mm of end bearing, is installed crown up, and is restrained at the bottom by strapping, bridging or a ceiling.
articles.why: Joists that are undersized, over-spanned or poorly supported cause bouncy floors, cracked tile and drywall, and doors that rub.
steps: Confirm size and spacing from the plans or span tables; check for point loads that need doubled joists or a beam.
Set joists crown up on the layout, flush with the rim.
Double joists under parallel partitions and around openings as required.
Where joists frame into a beam side, use hangers or ledgers.
Install bottom restraint (strapping, bridging or ceiling board) as required.
Lay out the joists so they clear toilet flanges, tub drains and duct runs where the plans show them.

tolerances.value: 38 mm minimum

tolerances.item: Joists framed into the side of a wood beam
tolerances.value: hangers, or a ledger of at least 38 x 64 mm

mistakes: A joist landing under a toilet flange or tub drain, then being cut.
Hangers with missing nails or the wrong nails.
Joists not doubled under a parallel bearing partition.
checkpoints: Hanger nailing complete; bearing lengths; no cut joists.
safety: Walking joists before the subfloor is on is a fall hazard; use planks and fall protection at height.

citations.note: spans for joists (span tables - not reproduced)

articles.title: Floor openings - trimmers, headers and tail joists
articles.summary: Openings for stairs, chimneys and chases are framed with trimmer joists along the sides and header joists across the ends; the shortened joists between are tail joists. Trimmers and headers are doubled when the opening is large, and long headers or tails hang in joist hangers.
articles.why: The trimmers and headers carry the load the cut joists would have carried. Under-built openings sag at the stair head.
steps: Mark the rough opening from the plans (stair openings must give the required headroom).
Install the inner trimmers, then the headers, then the tail joists, then double up.
Use hangers or the required end-nailing at header-to-trimmer and tail-to-header connections.

tolerances.item: Support of tail and header joists
tolerances.value: hangers or nailing per the code for the span of the header/tail

tolerances.item: Clear headroom over stairs in a house
tolerances.value: 1 950 mm minimum

mistakes: Stair opening too short - headroom fails at the third or fourth tread.
Single headers where doubling is required.
checkpoints: Headroom line checked before the opening is framed.

citations.note: support of tail and header joists

articles.title: Blocking, bridging and strapping
articles.summary: Blocking is short pieces fitted between joists or studs. It supports panel edges, transfers loads at bearing lines, stops joists rolling, backs up fixtures and acts as fire blocking. Bridging (cross or solid) and strapping restrain the joist bottoms and share load between joists.
articles.why: Missing blocking is one of the most common framing inspection items, and missing backing is the most common call-back from other trades.
steps: Install solid blocking at bearing over beams and walls where joists lap or where required for lateral support.
Add 38 x 38 mm or larger blocking under unsupported subfloor edges when T&G panels are not used.
Strap or bridge joist bottoms as required by the joist span and ceiling type.
Add fire blocking and fixture backing at the same pass - see the linked articles.

tolerances.value: tongue-and-groove edges or 38 x 38 mm blocking

mistakes: Blocks cut too long, pushing joists off layout and humping the subfloor.
Forgetting blocking at the top of walls running parallel to joists (needed for drywall and air barrier).
checkpoints: Blocking at panel edges, bearing lines and parallel-wall tops.

citations.note: blocking for air barrier continuity at interior walls

articles.title: Cantilevered floor joists
articles.summary: A cantilever is a joist that extends past its support, for a bay or overhang. Joists that carry roof loads may only cantilever a limited distance - 400 mm for 38 x 184 mm (2x8) joists and 600 mm for 38 x 235 mm (2x10) or larger - and may not carry floor loads from storeys above without calculation. Cantilevers at right angles to the main joists need tail joists that run back at least six times the cantilever length.
articles.why: Cantilevers are a common place for over-reach; the back-span is what holds them down.

tolerances.value: 400 mm / 600 mm maximum

tolerances.item: Back-span of perpendicular cantilever tail joists
tolerances.value: at least 6 x the cantilever length

mistakes: Cantilever carrying a wall and floor from above without an engineer.
Insulating and air-sealing the cantilever floor poorly - a cold floor and frozen pipes.
checkpoints: Cantilever length and back-span before sheathing.

articles.title: Subfloor - glue, nail and layout
articles.summary: The subfloor is the structural panel (plywood or OSB, usually T&G) over the joists. Panels go with their strength axis across the joists and end joints staggered, edges supported, glued with subfloor adhesive and fastened per the code. It becomes the platform for wall layout.
articles.why: A glued, well-fastened subfloor is the difference between a quiet floor and a squeaky one, and it braces the deck.
steps: Start with a full panel along a straight chalk line; groove edge toward the wall line as the maker directs.
Bead adhesive on each joist just ahead of the panel.
Stagger end joints over joists by at least one joist space.
Leave the expansion gap the maker specifies (typically about 3 mm).
Fasten with ring-shank nails or screws at the required spacing before the glue skins.

tolerances.value: strength axis at right angles to joists, end joints staggered
per the code fastener table for the panel thickness
about 3 mm, as printed on the panel

mistakes: Glue skinned over before the panel is laid.
Panels tight edge to edge - buckling when they take on moisture.
Nails missing the joists (shiners).
checkpoints: Fastener spacing and glue lines; no unsupported edges.

citations.note: Engineered Wood Construction Guide E30 - floors

articles.title: I-joists, LVL, glulam and trusses - follow the maker's guide
articles.summary: Engineered wood products (wood I-joists, LVL, LSL, glulam, metal-plate trusses) are designed and approved by their manufacturer. Span, bearing, web stiffeners, squash blocks, rim board and the allowed hole chart all come from that product's current installation guide, not from the lumber span tables. Never cut a flange or truss member.
articles.why: These products are efficient because they remove material where it is not needed. Cutting a flange, drilling outside the hole chart, or missing a web stiffener can drop capacity dramatically.
steps: Get the layout and the installation guide for the exact series and depth.
Install rim board, blocking panels, web stiffeners and squash blocks as detailed.
Use only the hangers listed for the product, nailed fully.
Drill holes only where the hole chart allows; knockouts are pre-scored for small holes.
Brace I-joists temporarily before walking on them.

tolerances.value: only per the manufacturer's hole chart; never in flanges
no notching or drilling unless allowed in the truss design

mistakes: Cutting I-joist flanges for drains or ducts.
Walking on unbraced I-joists - they roll and collapse.
Using sawn-lumber hangers on I-joists.
checkpoints: Web stiffeners, squash blocks and hanger nailing match the layout.
safety: Unbraced I-joists are a known cause of falls; install temporary bracing and sheathing as the maker directs.

citations.note: product installation guide for the specified series
roof trusses not notched or drilled unless designed

articles.title: Wall plates and layout
articles.summary: Each wall starts as a bottom plate and top plate laid side by side on the deck. All stud, opening and intersection locations are marked across both at once, so studs land square and on layout. Plates are the same width as the studs (38 x 89 or 38 x 140 mm) and the bottom plate of exterior walls is sealed to the subfloor.
articles.why: Layout done once on paired plates is fast and accurate; most stud-spacing and opening-location errors start here.
steps: Snap wall lines on the deck from the plan dimensions.
Cut plates, tack them side by side, and mark from one end - studs, kings, jacks, cripples, intersection backing and corner details.
Mark openings by their rough-opening centre lines from the window and door schedule.
Mark plumbing walls and duct chases so studs miss them.

tolerances.value: 400 or 600 mm on centre to match sheathing and drywall
at least the stud width, fastened to the floor per the nailing schedule

mistakes: Laying out from the wrong end so studs and sheathing joints do not line up.
Forgetting intersection backing (ladder blocking or channel) for drywall.
checkpoints: Plate layout against the plan before nailing studs.
tools: layout stick or tape with 16/24 in marks

citations.note: stud size and spacing (table not reproduced)

articles.title: Studs - size, spacing and corners
articles.summary: Studs are the vertical members of a wall. Size and spacing depend on the load carried and the wall height (a code table sets the limits). Common studs fill the layout, king studs run full height beside openings, and corners and intersections are built so there is backing for drywall and room for insulation.
articles.why: Studs carry the floors and roof above and support sheathing and finishes. The wrong size or spacing for the load is a structural failure; poor corners waste energy.
steps: Cut studs to the precut or plan length (wall height less plates).
Nail studs through the plates, crown all one way, on the layout marks.
Build insulated corners (two- or three-stud corners with drywall clips) where the energy design calls for it.
Stand, plumb, and brace the wall.

tolerances.value: per the code table for the supported loads and height

tolerances.item: Remaining depth after notching or drilling a loadbearing stud
tolerances.value: at least 2/3 of the depth
wide face perpendicular to the wall, except where flat studs are allowed

mistakes: 600 mm spacing used where the load needs 400.
Solid corners with no space for insulation.
Crowns alternating, giving wavy drywall.
checkpoints: Spacing, size and continuity of studs; no over-drilled studs.

articles.title: Headers (lintels) over openings - kings, jacks, cripples and sills
articles.summary: A header (the code calls it a lintel) carries the load over a window or door to the jack studs (trimmers) at each side, which sit beside full-height king studs. Cripple studs fill above the header and below the rough sill. Header size comes from the code lintel tables or a designer; openings with headers over 3 m long need tripled studs at each side.
articles.why: The header turns a uniform load from above into two point loads. If the header, its bearing or the jacks are undersized, the opening sags, windows bind and drywall cracks.
steps: Read the rough opening (RO) width and height from the window or door schedule.
Nail the king stud full height, then the jack stud(s) to it, cut to header height.
Build the header (two or three plies with insulation between, or an engineered header) and set it on the jacks tight to the kings.
Install the rough sill and cripples below, and cripples above the header on layout.
Check the RO size and that it is square (diagonals).

tolerances.value: from the code lintel span tables for the load case, or by design

tolerances.item: Openings with a lintel over 3 m
tolerances.value: studs tripled each side - two jacks under the lintel plus a king
window size plus about 12-19 mm each way, or per the window maker

mistakes: Header bearing on a single jack where two are needed.
No insulation in the header cavity - a cold spot and condensation.
Cripples off layout so sheathing and drywall joints miss.
checkpoints: Header size and bearing match the plan; RO size and square.

citations.note: lintel spans and sizes (tables not reproduced)

articles.title: Top plates and cap plates - laps and splices
articles.summary: Loadbearing walls need two top plates. The second (cap) plate is lapped over intersecting walls and corners to tie them together, and joints in top plates are staggered by at least one stud space (more where many nails are needed). A single top plate is only allowed in limited cases.
articles.why: The doubled, lapped top plate ties walls into one frame and spreads joist and rafter loads that do not land on a stud.
steps: Stand all walls on the level before capping, so caps can lap at every corner and intersection.
Lap the cap plate over the joint below by at least one stud space and nail per the schedule.
Keep the cap plate width at least 50 mm after any notches or holes, or reinforce with a strap.

tolerances.item: Number of top plates in loadbearing walls
tolerances.value: two, except in the specific cases allowed
at least one stud spacing, more with heavier nailing

tolerances.item: Remaining width of a top plate after holes or notches
tolerances.value: 50 mm minimum, otherwise reinforce

mistakes: Butt joints in both plates at the same stud.
Plumber or electrician cutting the full plate width without a strap.
checkpoints: Laps at all intersections; straps over cut plates.

articles.title: Wall bracing and braced wall panels
articles.summary: Walls resist wind and earthquake racking with braced wall panels - usually wood structural panel sheathing nailed at the required spacing - arranged in braced wall bands. How much bracing is needed depends on the wind and seismic hazard of the location; much of coastal BC is in the higher seismic categories, where the code adds requirements or sends the design to an engineer.
articles.why: Without bracing a house racks sideways in an earthquake or wind storm. In high seismic zones the details (panel length, nailing, hold-downs, anchor bolts) matter as much as the panels.
steps: Confirm the location's wind and seismic category from the plans or climatic data.
Locate braced wall bands and panels as drawn; keep panels at least the minimum length.
Nail sheathing at the required edge and field spacing; blocking at unsupported edges where required.
Install the required anchor bolts at each braced panel end in high seismic areas.
Temporary bracing holds walls plumb until sheathing is complete.

tolerances.value: location, length and materials per the code for the hazard level
additional requirements or engineering design

mistakes: Window or door openings placed where the braced panel needs full-height sheathing.
Over-driven nails that break the panel surface.
checkpoints: Panel nailing, panel lengths and anchor bolts before cladding covers them.

citations.note: low to moderate wind and seismic
braced wall panels in braced wall bands

articles.title: Seismic design in BC houses - when Part 9 needs an engineer
articles.summary: Much of southwest BC has high seismic hazard. Part 9 adds braced-wall and anchorage requirements above certain seismic values (for example extra anchor bolts at braced panels where Smax for Site Class C exceeds 0.47), and beyond the extreme-hazard limits the lateral design must be done by a structural engineer. HASWORKS HOMES flags these houses and imports the engineer's design rather than inventing it.
articles.why: Seismic detailing is invisible once drywall goes on, and it is where Part 9 prescriptive rules stop.
steps: Read the seismic values for the site from the climatic and seismic data for the municipality.
If over the Part 9 limits, get a structural engineer's lateral design and schedules.
Frame and nail exactly to the engineer's schedule; hold-downs and anchors are inspected.

tolerances.item: Anchor bolts at braced wall panels where Smax (Site Class C) > 0.47
tolerances.value: at least two per panel, near the panel ends, at the table spacing
engineering design required

mistakes: Treating a high-seismic lot like a low-seismic one because the house is small.
checkpoints: Engineer's field review letters (Schedules) before cover-up.
articles.signoff: Structural engineer (P.Eng.) where the Part 9 seismic limits are exceeded

citations.note: anchorage of building frames, seismic case
requirements for high wind and seismic forces
requirements for extreme wind and seismic forces

articles.title: Wall sheathing
articles.summary: Exterior wall sheathing (OSB or plywood, sometimes rigid insulation where structural bracing is provided otherwise) backs the cladding and often forms the braced wall panels. Panels are installed with gaps, edges on framing, and fastened at the required spacing; panel joints over openings are kept off the corners of the opening.
articles.why: Sheathing carries racking loads and is the substrate for the sheathing membrane and cladding fasteners.
steps: Sheathe walls flat on the deck where possible - faster and safer.
Keep a 3 mm gap at panel edges and ends.
Fasten at the required edge and field spacing, more where the panel is a braced wall panel.
Cut openings after nailing; do not land a panel joint on the line of a header corner.

tolerances.value: per code minimums for the stud spacing
gapped and supported per the code

mistakes: Panel joints in line with header corners - cracks in stucco or siding later.
Nails missing studs.
checkpoints: Nailing pattern and edge distance on braced panels.
tools: router with flush bit for openings

articles.title: Notching and drilling limits for joists, studs and plates
articles.summary: Holes in floor, roof and ceiling members may be no larger than one quarter of the member depth and must stay at least 50 mm from the edges. Notches are allowed only on the top edge, within half the depth from the bearing, and no deeper than one third of the depth. Loadbearing studs must keep at least 2/3 of their depth (40 mm for non-loadbearing). Top plates must keep 50 mm. Trusses and engineered joists follow their own design.
articles.why: Trades cut more structure than framers do. These limits keep the member strong enough; beyond them the member must be made deeper, reinforced, or redesigned.
steps: Plan service routes before drilling - HASWORKS HOMES shows designed hole locations on the cut list.
Drill near the middle of the depth, away from bearing points and away from the top and bottom edges.
Check the hole against the limit for that member size (see the table below).
If a pipe or duct cannot fit, change the route, add a chase, or have the member reinforced by design.

tolerances.item: Max hole diameter in a joist, 2x8 / 2x10 / 2x12 (184 / 235 / 286 mm deep)
tolerances.value: 46 / 58 / 71 mm, at least 50 mm from edges

tolerances.item: Max top notch depth, 2x8 / 2x10 / 2x12, within half the depth of the bearing

tolerances.value: at least 60 / 94 mm (2/3 of 89 / 140 mm, rounded up)
at least 40 mm
at least 50 mm, otherwise reinforce
only per the manufacturer's hole chart or truss design

mistakes: A 3 in drain (about 89 mm outside diameter) through a 2x10 joist - well over the 58 mm limit.
Notching the bottom edge of a joist.
Clusters of holes close together in one stud.
checkpoints: Framing inspection looks at every cut member; reinforcement where limits are exceeded.
safety: Right-angle drills can kick violently when a bit binds; use the side handle and the clutch.

articles.title: Nailing schedule and fasteners for framing
articles.summary: The code nailing table sets the minimum number and length of nails for each framing connection (stud to plate, joist to sill, rafter to plate and so on). Nails must meet the nail standard; galvanized or stainless fasteners are used with treated wood; and fasteners near ends are placed to avoid splitting. Screws and connectors are allowed where they give the same strength.
articles.why: Connections are where most framing failures start. Gun nails are often shorter and thinner than hand nails - check the equivalent.
steps: Use the code table (or the engineer's schedule) for each connection type.
Check gun nail length and diameter against the required nail.
Use hot-dip galvanized or stainless fasteners and connectors with treated lumber.
Pre-drill or blunt nails near ends to prevent splitting.

tolerances.value: number and length of nails per the code nailing table
corrosion-resistant, compatible with the treatment

mistakes: Clipped-head or undersized gun nails substituted without checking.
Electro-galvanized nails in treated sill plates.
checkpoints: Nail counts at key connections (rafter-to-plate, joist-to-sill, hanger nailing).

articles.title: Rafters, ridge, ceiling joists and ties
articles.summary: In a stick-framed roof, rafters run from the wall plate to the ridge. Opposite rafters either meet directly or are offset by their thickness on a ridge board at least 17.5 mm thick. The outward push of the rafters is resisted by ceiling joists or rafter ties at the plate, or by a structural ridge beam. Collar ties near the peak stiffen the pair. Rafters and joists need at least 38 mm of bearing.
articles.why: An untied rafter roof pushes the walls apart and the ridge sags. The tie is what turns two rafters and a ceiling joist into a triangle.
steps: Confirm rafter and ridge size from span tables or the designer; decide ridge board vs structural ridge.
Cut a pattern rafter (plumb cut, birdsmouth seat, tail) and test it at both ends of the roof.
Set the ridge at height, then rafter pairs from the ends in, on layout over the studs.
Nail ceiling joists or rafter ties to each rafter heel per the nailing table.
Add collar ties, then roof sheathing.

tolerances.item: End bearing of rafters and joists
tolerances.value: 38 mm minimum

tolerances.item: Ridge board where rafters are offset
tolerances.value: 17.5 mm thick minimum; rafters offset no more than their thickness
no deeper than about 1/3 of the rafter depth

mistakes: Cathedral ceiling with a ridge board instead of a structural ridge beam - no tie, walls spread.
Over-cut birdsmouths weakening the rafter at the wall.
Ceiling joists not nailed to the rafters at the heel.
checkpoints: Rafter-to-ceiling-joist nailing, ridge support, tie spacing.
safety: Roof framing is work at height - guardrails or fall arrest per WorkSafeBC Part 11.

citations.note: intermediate support for rafters and joists

articles.title: Roof trusses - delivery, setting and bracing
articles.summary: Most BC houses use metal-plate-connected wood trusses designed by the truss supplier. The truss layout and design drawings say where each truss goes, its bearing and the permanent bracing. Trusses must not be cut, notched or drilled unless the design allows, and they need temporary and permanent bracing while being set.
articles.why: Trusses are strong in their plane and weak out of it. Most truss collapses during construction come from missing temporary bracing.
steps: Check the delivered trusses against the layout and design sheets.
Set gable ends and the first truss braced to the ground or the deck.
Set trusses on layout, fastening each to the plate with the specified connector.
Install temporary lateral and diagonal bracing as you go, then permanent bracing as designed.

tolerances.value: none unless covered by the truss design
per the truss design drawings

mistakes: Cutting a truss chord to fit an attic hatch or duct.
Removing temporary bracing before sheathing and permanent bracing are complete.
checkpoints: Truss design sheets on site; permanent bracing installed; connectors at each bearing.

articles.title: Roof sheathing and panel clips

articles.title: Stairs - rise, run, headroom and stringers
articles.summary: Stairs inside a house are private stairs. Each rise must be between 125 and 200 mm and each run between 255 and 355 mm, with risers uniform within 5 mm of each other and 10 mm across a flight. Headroom must be at least 1 950 mm in a single dwelling. Stringers are cut from wide lumber and keep enough wood below the cut.
articles.why: Uneven risers are a leading cause of falls. The finished floor thickness at the top and bottom is the usual reason a stair ends up out of tolerance.
steps: Measure total rise from finished floor to finished floor (account for flooring thicknesses).
Divide into equal risers within the limits; pick a run that suits the space.
Lay out stringers with a framing square and stair gauges; cut one, test it, then copy.
Drop the bottom of the stringer by the tread thickness so the first and last risers come out equal.
Fasten stringers at the top (hanger or ledger) and at the bottom.

articles.title: Guards and handrails
articles.summary: A guard is required where a walking surface is more than 600 mm above the surface beside it. Inside a dwelling guards must be at least 900 mm high (1 070 mm elsewhere, with exceptions for low exterior decks), and openings must stop a 100 mm sphere. Required handrails are 865 to 1 070 mm high and need clearance behind them for a hand.
articles.why: Guards and handrails prevent falls, especially for children - the 100 mm sphere rule is about a child's head.

Anchor guard posts per the designed connection; loads on guards are specified by the code.
Check heights from the nosing line on stairs and from the floor on landings.

articles.title: Backing for fixtures, cabinets, grab bars and finishes
articles.summary: Backing is solid blocking set in the wall or ceiling during framing so later items have something to screw into - upper and lower cabinets, wall-hung toilets and vanities, towel bars, grab bars, TV mounts, handrails, shower doors, curtain rods and ceiling fans. articles.title: How HASWORKS HOMES labels its guidance (and what still needs a designer)
articles.summary: Every rule, article and value in HASWORKS HOMES carries one of four labels. Code-required means a clause of the building, plumbing or electrical code sets it. Manufacturer means the product's installation instructions set it and they override general guidance. Best practice is trade knowledge that is not a code minimum. Needs sign-off means an engineer, designer or the authority having jurisdiction must approve it before you build.
articles.why: Generated framing (computed spans, sizes and connections) is a starting point, not a stamped design. Knowing which label applies tells you whether you can build from it, must check the product sheet, or must wait for a sign-off.
steps: Read the label chip on the piece, step or rule before cutting.
For any piece flagged "GENERATED" or "computed span", confirm the size against the approved drawings, span tables or the designer's schedule.
For manufacturer items, have the product's current installation guide on site.
For needs-sign-off items, get the engineer's or designer's letter or field review before cover-up.
Record the confirmation in the build log so the next crew sees it.
mistakes: Treating a generated size as approved because it looks right.
Using a best-practice value where the code sets a stricter minimum.
Covering engineered items before the engineer's field review.
checkpoints: Before framing inspection - every needs-sign-off item has its letter or review on file.

articles.title: Electrical permits and inspections in BC
articles.summary: Electrical work in BC is regulated under the Safety Standards Act. The BC Electrical Code is the Canadian Electrical Code Part I, 26th edition (C22.1:24), in force for permits issued after March 4, 2025. Permits come from Technical Safety BC, or from the city where it has delegated authority (for example Vancouver, Surrey, Burnaby, Victoria). Work is done by a licensed electrical contractor, or by a homeowner under a homeowner permit for their own home, and is inspected at rough-in before cover-up.
articles.why: Covering wiring before the rough-in inspection means opening walls.
steps: Confirm who issues permits for the address (Technical Safety BC or the city).
Take out the permit before starting; declare the code edition if the permit straddles the change-over.
Book the rough-in inspection after boxes, cables and bonding are in and before insulation.
Final inspection after devices and the panel are complete.

articles.title: Outlet and switch box layout and heights

Typical BC heights are receptacles about 400 mm to centre, switches about 1 100-1 200 mm to centre, and counter receptacles about 1 070-1 100 mm. articles.title: Running cable through framing - bore holes and nail plates
articles.summary: Non-metallic sheathed cable (NMD90) run through studs and joists goes in bored holes set back from the face of the member, or is protected by a steel plate where it is closer to the edge, so drywall screws and trim nails cannot reach it. Holes also have to respect the framing limits (hole size and edge distance). HASWORKS HOMES lays out designed bore holes on the cut list so the saw marks them before the wall is built.
articles.why: Screws through cables cause shocks and fires years later. Random holes weaken studs and joists.
steps: Plan cable routes along the designed bore line (typically the middle of the stud).
Drill straight, same height, deburr; avoid the top and bottom of joists.
Install nail plates wherever a cable is closer to the face than the code allows.
Staple within the required distance of boxes and at intervals; do not over-drive staples.

articles.title: Drain, waste and vent (DWV) basics - slope, traps and vents
articles.summary: The DWV system carries waste by gravity and keeps trap seals in place with vents. Horizontal drains slope continuously toward the building drain - typically 1 in 50 (2%, about 1/4 in per foot) for 3 in and smaller - every fixture has a trap, and every trap is vented within the allowed trap-arm length. Cleanouts are placed so every line can be rodded.
articles.why: Too little slope clogs, too much leaves solids behind, and an unvented trap siphons dry and lets sewer gas into the house.
steps: Lay out stacks and drains on the plan first, then confirm framing clears them (see framing for drains).
Hang horizontal pipe at a uniform slope with proper supports.
Install traps at each fixture, with vents within the allowed trap-arm length.
Provide cleanouts at the base of stacks and changes of direction as required.
Test the system before cover (see plumbing tests).

articles.title: Framing for plumbing - toilets, tubs, stacks and big drains
articles.summary: Most plumbing damage to framing happens because the layout did not plan for drains. A 3 in (75 mm) drain has an outside diameter of about 89 mm - far bigger than the 58 mm hole a 2x10 joist allows. HASWORKS HOMES checks the plan's fixtures against the joist layout so no joist lands under a toilet flange or tub drain, runs drains parallel to joists, and adds 2x6 wet walls or chases for stacks.
articles.why: Solving the drain route on the plan is free; solving it with a saw is a structural repair.

Shift joists or add headers so they clear drains; use 2x6 (38 x 140) plumbing walls for 3 in stacks.
Run horizontal drains parallel to joists or in a dropped ceiling or chase.
Where a joist must be cut, frame a header and trimmers as for a floor opening, or have an engineered solution.

articles.title: Before you dig - BC 1 Call locates and utility safety
articles.summary: Before any excavation, request utility locates through BC 1 Call and wait for every utility to respond. Locates mark buried gas, power, telecom and some water and sewer lines; private lines (to a garage, a well or a septic field) are not marked and need a private locator.
articles.why: Striking a gas or power line kills workers. It is also the most expensive way to delay a job.
steps: Submit a locate request with the dig area outlined, several working days before digging.
Confirm every listed utility has responded and keep the locate sheets on site.

articles.title: Site layout, batter boards and elevations
articles.summary: Layout transfers the surveyor's property pins and the plan's setbacks and elevations to the ground. Batter boards with string lines set the building corners and wall lines; a benchmark elevation (a geodetic or site datum) sets footing, top-of-wall and main-floor heights. The HASWORKS HOMES Site view places the house on the real terrain and lists the target elevations.
articles.why: A house built in the wrong place or at the wrong height cannot be fixed. Municipal setback and height limits are checked from the survey.
steps: Have a BC land surveyor stake the corners and provide a benchmark; keep the survey certificate.
Set batter boards beyond the excavation; run strings for the outside of the foundation.
Check diagonals (or the 3-4-5 method) for square.
Transfer elevations with a laser level from the benchmark; mark top of footing and top of wall.

Dig to the footing elevation and to undisturbed soil; do not over-dig.

Keep water out (pumps, ditches) and protect the bottom from frost.

articles.title: Backfill

Keep heavy equipment back from the wall.

articles.title: Radon and soil gas - the rough-in every house needs
articles.summary: Radon is a radioactive soil gas and the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers. BCBC requires floors-on-ground to have an air barrier against soil gas and a rough-in for a future subfloor depressurization system - a sealed radon vent pipe through the slab into a gas-permeable layer (for example 100 mm of clean coarse granular). Health Canada's guideline is 200 Bq/m3; test after occupancy.
articles.why: The rough-in costs little during construction and makes fixing a high-radon house simple.
steps: Place at least 100 mm of clean coarse granular under the slab.
Install the soil-gas barrier (polyethylene) lapped and sealed at joints and penetrations, and sealed to the foundation.
Install the radon vent pipe with its inlet in the gas-permeable layer, capped and labelled.
Seal all slab penetrations and the slab-to-wall joint.
Recommend a long-term radon test (3 months, in the heating season) to the owner.

Pipe left open or unlabelled.

articles.title: Concrete floor slab (floor-on-ground)
articles.summary: A basement or slab-on-grade floor is placed over at least 100 mm of clean coarse granular, a soil-gas barrier, and usually rigid insulation for Step Code houses. Slabs are at least 75 mm thick, with a bond break at footings, and under-slab plumbing and radon pipe are inspected before the pour.
articles.why: The granular layer drains and lets soil gas be vented; the slab is the air barrier at the bottom of the house.
steps: Rough-in under-slab plumbing and get it tested and inspected.
Place and compact granular; install insulation and poly as designed.
Pour, finish and cure; cut or tool control joints within a day.

No insulation edge break where the energy design needs one.

articles.title: Anchor bolts, sill gasket and sill plates
articles.summary: The sill plate (at least 38 x 89 mm, pressure treated or separated from the concrete) sits on the foundation and is fastened with anchor bolts at least 12.7 mm in diameter, no more than 2.4 m apart - closer, and at each braced wall panel end, in high seismic areas. It must be level (on mortar or on a level wall) and the joint to the foundation is sealed as part of the air barrier.
articles.why: The sill is where the house is tied down against wind and earthquakes, and a major air-leakage and moisture point.
steps: Check the wall top for level and straight; grout low spots.
Roll out the sill gasket (foam or EPDM) on the concrete.
Mark and drill the sill for the anchor bolts; bolts within about 300 mm of each sill end is good practice.
Set the sill, add washers and nuts, and tighten.

No gasket, leaving an air leak the length of the house.

articles.title: Crawl spaces - heated vs unheated
articles.summary: An unheated crawl space is outside the insulated envelope - the floor above is insulated and the crawl space is vented. A heated crawl space is inside the envelope - its walls are insulated, it is not vented to outside, and it gets conditioned air or ventilation. Both need an access opening, drainage, and a ground cover (soil-gas barrier).
articles.why: Mixing the two approaches (insulating the walls and venting to outside) causes condensation and mould.

tolerances.value: required, sized per the code
unheated - vented to outside; heated - ventilated as part of the house
required, sealed in heated crawl spaces

mistakes: Venting a heated crawl space to the outside.
Leaving soil exposed.
