terms.plain: The BC Energy Step Code - performance steps for new buildings in BCBC 9.36.6; Step 3 is the provincial minimum for houses, with higher steps by local bylaw.
BCBC Section 9.37 - greenhouse-gas emission levels for new buildings, chosen by local government.
An NRCan-registered professional who models the house, runs blower door tests and files Step Code reports.
Thermal energy demand and total energy use intensity metrics used in Step Code; houses now use percent improvement metrics.
How much less energy the modelled house uses than the code reference house - a Step Code target.
Step Code target for how much the envelope reduces heat loss compared to the reference house.
Greenhouse gas intensity - kg CO2e per m2 per year; one metric in the Zero Carbon Step Code.
A calibrated fan mounted in a doorway that depressurizes the house to measure air leakage.
Air changes per hour at 50 Pa - how many times the house air volume leaks out per hour during a blower door test.
Normalized leakage area at 10 Pa, in cm2 per m2 of envelope area; a BC airtightness metric suited to small homes.
Normalized leakage rate at 50 Pa, in L/s per m2 of envelope area.
Band of heating degree-days used by 9.36 - Zone 4 under 3 000 HDD up to Zone 8 at 7 000 or more.
Material placed in a concealed space to stop fire and smoke spreading through it.
A hidden space inside walls, floors, ceilings or attics through which fire could travel unseen.
A construction assembly that acts as a barrier against fire spread, e.g. between a house and a secondary suite.
Sealed against the passage of exhaust gases, as required between an attached garage and the house.
A door fitted with a closer or spring hinges so it shuts by itself.
A self-contained detector and sounder that warns occupants of smoke; required on every storey and in bedrooms.
Smoke alarms wired (or linked) so that when one sounds, all sound.
Carbon monoxide alarm - required where a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage serves the house.
Panels of gypsum between paper faces used for interior walls and ceilings.
Fire-rated gypsum board with glass fibres that holds together longer in a fire.
Sprayed ceiling finish; water-based texture adds weight and moisture, so supports must be closer.
A bedroom window big enough and easy enough to open to escape through - 0.35 m2, no side under 380 mm.
Systems that prevent or arrest falls - guardrails, covers, travel restraint or fall arrest. Required from 3 m in BC.
A temporary rail system on floor edges and openings during construction - a top rail and mid rail meeting WorkSafeBC specs.
A harness and lanyard set so the worker cannot reach the edge.
A harness, lanyard and anchor that stop a worker after they fall.
Temporary supports that hold excavation walls back.
Cutting excavation walls into steps to reduce collapse risk.
Excavated soil piled beside the hole; kept back from the edge.
Respirable crystalline silica dust from cutting concrete, stone and fibre-cement; causes silicosis.
A written plan for controlling worker exposure to a hazard such as silica dust.
A nailer that fires only when the nose is pressed and then the trigger pulled, reducing accidental double shots.
Sudden backward jump of a saw when the blade binds.
An array of infrared beams that stops a machine instantly when a person reaches into the danger zone; used on the Acucut by HASWORKS HOMES cutting cell.
Local government approval to build; drawings, energy report and any engineer's schedules are submitted for it.
BC forms in which registered professionals take responsibility for design (Schedule B) and field review (Schedule C-B).
An architect or engineer registered in BC who designs and field-reviews regulated work.
A builder licensed by BC Housing under the Homeowner Protection Act to build new homes.
A person authorized by BC Housing to build a home for their own use without home warranty insurance, with disclosure rules on sale.
Mandatory third-party warranty insurance on new BC homes - 2 years materials and labour, 5 years envelope, 10 years structure.
A stage that must be inspected and passed before work can cover it up.
Final approval from the local government that the house can be lived in.
Wall design with a drained and vented cavity behind the cladding so water that gets past the siding drains out and the wall dries.
Water-resistive barrier - the sheathing membrane behind cladding that sheds water while letting vapour out.
A gap or drainage layer that stops water wicking from the back of the cladding into the wall - e.g. a drained, vented space at least 9.5 mm deep.
The cladding and its joints - the outer surface that sheds most rain.
The drainage cavity, sheathing membrane and flashings behind the cladding that deal with water that gets past it.
The exterior finish of the wall - siding, stucco, brick, panels.
Strips fastened to a wall or ceiling to create a space or a flat nailing surface for finishes or cladding.
Sheet metal or membrane that directs water out of a joint and away from the wall or roof.
A flashing edge bent out and down so water drips clear of the surface below.
A diverter at the bottom of a roof-to-wall junction that throws water into the gutter instead of behind the cladding.
Z-shaped flashing at a horizontal joint between cladding panels or materials.
Sloped, sealed membrane or formed pan at the bottom of a rough opening with end dams and a back dam.
An upturned edge at the inside of a window sill pan that stops water running into the house.
Flashing over the top of a window or door that sends water out over the frame.
The perimeter fin on a window frame that is fastened to the sheathing and integrated with membranes.
Peel-and-stick membrane (modified bitumen or butyl/acrylic) used for sill pans, flashing and eave protection.
The materials and joints that together stop air leaking through the envelope; must be continuous.
An air barrier approach where interior drywall, sealed to framing with gaskets or sealant, forms the air barrier.
Non-hardening sealant used to seal polyethylene laps and the air barrier to framing.
A layer of low vapour permeance on the warm side that limits moisture diffusion into the wall.
How easily water vapour passes through a material, in ng/(Pa s m2). Vapour barriers have low permeance.
The temperature at which air's moisture condenses. Keep the dew point outside materials that can rot.
Metric thermal resistance in m2 K/W. RSI x 5.678 = R-value.
Imperial thermal resistance (ft2 F h/Btu). R-20 is about RSI 3.52.
The thermal resistance of the whole assembly including framing and thermal bridges, not just the insulation label.
Heat flowing faster through framing, concrete or metal that interrupts the insulation.
Pre-cut piece of fibreglass or mineral wool insulation sized for stud or joist cavities.
A channel at the eave that keeps attic insulation from blocking soffit vents.
Openings at the eaves and ridge that let outside air move through the attic to remove moisture.
Vent in the underside of the roof overhang that lets air into the attic.
Continuous vent at the roof peak that lets attic air out.
Electrical box with a flange and gasket that can be sealed to the air barrier.
A tested product or system that seals a penetration through a fire separation so it keeps its rating.
Waterproof membrane at the roof eaves that stops ice-dam water leaking into the house.
A ridge of ice at the eave formed when heat leaking into the attic melts snow that refreezes at the cold overhang.
Sheet laid on the roof deck under the roofing (synthetic or felt), or a panel under finished flooring.
Heating degree-days below 18 C, summed over a year; a measure of how cold a place is. Vancouver is about 2 800, Prince George about 4 700.
The first course at the eave (and often rakes) that seals under the first exposed shingle course.
The part of a shingle or siding board left exposed to the weather.
How far a shingle course overlaps the course two below.
The printed or sealant strip on a shingle where nails must go for wind resistance.
Shingles or formed pieces covering the ridge and hips.
Individual L-shaped flashings woven with each shingle course where a roof meets a sidewall.
Flashing set into or over a wall or chimney that laps over the base or step flashing.
The internal angle where two roof planes meet, which carries the most water on a roof.
A small peaked roof built behind a chimney to divert water around it.
The usual Canadian framing method: each floor is built as a deck (platform), and the walls for that storey are framed on it. Plates at every floor act as fire blocks.
Older method where studs run continuously from the sill to the roof past the floors. Needs added fire blocking at each floor; rare in new houses except tall gable walls.
The route a load takes from the roof down through rafters, walls, headers, joists, beams, posts and footings to the soil. Every piece must bear on something that carries it.
The finished floor platform (joists plus subfloor) that walls are framed on. Not to be confused with an exterior deck.
The trade name of a lumber size (2x4, 2x10). The real dressed size is smaller, e.g. a 2x4 is 38 x 89 mm.
The actual size of lumber after planing - 38 mm thick for 2-by lumber; 89, 140, 184, 235 and 286 mm wide for 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 inch nominal.
The mark on each piece of structural lumber showing the grading agency, mill, species group, grade and moisture condition (e.g. S-P-F No.2 S-DRY).
Surfaced dry - lumber dried to 19% moisture content or less before planing. KD means kiln dried; S-GRN means surfaced green (wet).
Spruce-Pine-Fir, the species group that supplies most Canadian framing lumber. Span tables list values by species group.
The slight curve along the edge of a board. Joists, rafters and headers are installed crown up so loads flatten them.
Lumber impregnated with preservative to resist decay and insects. Used for sills on concrete, near grade and outdoors; needs compatible corrosion-resistant fasteners.
A horizontal member that carries joists over a span and puts the load onto posts or walls.
A beam made by nailing two or more 38 mm members together on edge. Butt joints must fall over supports.
A vertical member (wood, steel column or built-up studs) carrying a concentrated load from a beam or header down to a footing.
The length of a member that rests on its support. The code sets minimums, e.g. 38 mm for joists and rafters and 89 mm for beams.
Laminated veneer lumber - engineered beam stock made of glued veneers. Used for headers and beams; sized by the maker's tables.
Glued-laminated timber - a beam made of many glued lumber laminations, often exposed in post-and-beam work.
The joist around the outside edge of a floor that closes off the joist ends and carries the wall above.
Spacing measured from the centre of one member to the centre of the next, e.g. studs at 400 mm (16 in) o.c.
Marking the position of every stud, joist or rafter on plates or rims before nailing, usually with symbols for kings, jacks and cripples.
Horizontal framing member that carries the floor, spanning between foundation walls, beams and bearing walls.
The clear distance a member covers between supports. Allowed spans come from span tables for the species, grade, size, spacing and load.
Galvanized steel connector that supports a joist end against a beam or header. Every nail hole the maker specifies must be filled with the specified nail.
Diagonal or solid pieces between joists that keep them upright and share load. Cross-bridging is metal or wood X-braces.
Thin boards (often 19 x 64 mm) nailed across the underside of joists to restrain them, or vertically on walls to form a rainscreen cavity.
A joist (often doubled) along the side of a floor opening, carrying the headers.
In a floor, the member across the end of an opening that carries the tail joists. Also used for the rim joist at joist ends.
A shortened joist running from a header to a support, e.g. between a stair opening and a wall.
Clear height over a stair measured up from the line of the nosings. At least 1 950 mm in a single dwelling.
Short framing pieces fitted between joists or studs to support edges, stop rotation, back fixtures or block fire paths.
Blocking placed specifically so a later item - cabinet, grab bar, handrail, TV mount, drywall edge - has wood to fasten into.
Part of a joist or beam that projects past its support, such as a bay window floor or overhang.
Structural panels (plywood or OSB) fastened over joists, usually glued, forming the floor deck.
Oriented strand board - a structural panel of wood strands in cross-oriented layers, used for sheathing and subfloor.
Structural panel of cross-laminated veneers. Douglas fir (DFP) and Canadian softwood (CSP) are the common grades.
Panel or board edge profile where one edge locks into the next, supporting the joint without blocking.
The direction in which a structural panel is strongest (along the face grain or strand orientation). It must run across the supports.
Engineered joist with lumber or LVL flanges and an OSB web. Holes only per the maker's chart; flanges never cut.
Blocks nailed to both sides of an I-joist web at bearings or hangers so the web does not buckle.
Short lumber pieces beside an I-joist at a bearing that carry the wall load above past the joist.
A pre-engineered triangulated frame of lumber joined with metal plates, used for roofs and sometimes floors.
The upper (sloped) members of a roof truss, which carry the sheathing.
The lower horizontal member of a truss, which also forms the ceiling.
The diagonal and vertical pieces inside a truss between the chords.
The triangular end wall of a gable roof, often a special gable-end truss with studs for sheathing.
A multi-ply truss that carries other trusses on hangers, e.g. at a hip or a large opening.
The horizontal member at the bottom of a wall that the studs are nailed to and that is fastened to the floor.
The horizontal member at the top of a wall. Loadbearing walls usually have two.
The second top plate, lapped over corners and intersecting walls to tie them together.
A joint where two members are joined end to end with laps, plates or straps to act as one.
The framed opening for a window or door, slightly larger than the unit to allow shimming and sealing.
A vertical wall member between the plates.
A full-height stud on the regular layout, as opposed to kings, jacks or cripples.
A full-height stud at each side of an opening, nailed to the jack stud and the ends of the header.
A shortened stud beside the king that supports the end of a header.
A short stud above a header or below a rough sill, kept on layout for sheathing and drywall.
The beam over a window or door opening that carries the load above to the jack studs. The code calls it a lintel.
The horizontal framing member at the bottom of a window rough opening.
An insulated wall corner using two or three studs arranged so the corner cavity can be insulated, with clips or a stud for drywall backing.
Studs sold cut to a standard length (e.g. 92 5/8 in) so a wall with a single bottom and double top plate gives a standard ceiling height.
Framing that uses less lumber (600 mm spacing, single headers where allowed, two-stud corners, aligned framing) to leave more room for insulation.
A length of wall sheathed and nailed to resist racking from wind and earthquakes.
A continuous strip through a storey within which braced wall panels must be located.
Sideways distortion of a wall or building into a parallelogram under wind or earthquake load.
An engineered wall designed to resist lateral loads, with specified sheathing, nailing and hold-downs.
Steel connector anchoring the end post of a shear wall or braced panel to the floor or foundation against uplift.
How strong the design earthquake shaking is at a site. In Part 9 it decides which bracing and anchorage rules apply, or whether an engineer is needed.
Structural panels fastened to the outside of walls or the top of rafters and trusses.
The 3 mm space left between sheathing or subfloor panels so they can swell without buckling.
A small metal clip between roof sheathing panels that supports unblocked edges.
Plywood or OSB panels over rafters or trusses that carry roofing and brace the roof.
A piece cut out of the edge of a framing member. Joist notches are only allowed on the top edge near the bearing.
A hole drilled through a framing member for a pipe, wire or duct. Joist holes are limited to 1/4 of the depth and 50 mm from the edges.
The vertical (deep) dimension of a joist or rafter, or the wall-thickness dimension of a stud - the number hole and notch limits are based on.
Standard smooth-shank wire nail with a flat head; the reference nail in code nailing tables.
Nail driven at an angle through the side of one member into another, e.g. joist to sill.
Nail driven through one member into the end grain of another, e.g. bottom plate into stud.
Nail driven through the face of one member into the face of another, e.g. king stud to jack stud.
Metal connector that ties a rafter or truss to the wall plate against uplift.
A sloped roof framing member running from the wall plate to the ridge.
A non-structural board at the peak that rafters bear against; needs ceiling joists or ties to resist rafter thrust.
A structural beam at the peak, supported by posts, that carries half of each rafter's load - used for cathedral ceilings without ties.
The notch cut in a rafter where it sits on the wall plate - a level seat cut and a plumb cut.
Horizontal member carrying the ceiling that also ties the rafter heels together.
A horizontal piece connecting a pair of rafters in the upper part of the roof to stiffen them.
A tie low in the roof (at or near the plate) that resists the outward thrust of the rafters when ceiling joists do not.
A horizontal member across rafters or trusses, either to support them mid-span or to carry roofing.
The vertical height of one step, measured nosing to nosing. Private stairs - 125 to 200 mm.
The horizontal depth of one step, measured nosing to nosing. Private stairs - 255 to 355 mm.
Finished floor to finished floor height a stair climbs; divided into equal risers.
The front edge of a tread, sometimes projecting past the riser below.
The sloped member that supports the treads and risers of a stair, usually cut from 2x12 lumber.
A tapered tread used to turn a stair; allowed in houses within strict geometry limits.
A protective barrier at the edge of a floor, stair, deck or landing where the drop is more than 600 mm.
The rail people hold on a stair or ramp, 865 to 1 070 mm high where required.
A vertical infill piece in a guard; spaced so a 100 mm sphere cannot pass.
The main post at the start, end or turn of a stair handrail or guard.
A bar anchored to backing near a toilet, tub or shower to help people steady themselves.
A horizontal board fastened to a wall or beam to support joist ends; a deck ledger attaches an exterior deck to the house and needs flashing.
A framed vertical or horizontal space for ducts, pipes or flues; must be fire blocked.
A framed and drywalled box below a ceiling that hides a duct trunk, beam or pipes.
A wall that holds the main drain, vent and supply pipes; usually framed with 2x6 studs for a 3 in stack.
The stage when pipes, wires, boxes and ducts are installed in open framing, before insulation and drywall; also the inspection at that stage.
Canadian Electrical Code, Part I (CSA C22.1). The 2024 (26th) edition is the BC Electrical Code from March 4, 2025.
A business licensed by Technical Safety BC to do regulated electrical work, with a Field Safety Representative (FSR) responsible for it.
A permit that lets an owner do electrical work on their own home, subject to conditions and inspection.
The box that holds a switch or receptacle and the wire splices, fastened to framing.
The code term for an outlet you plug into.
The limit on how many conductors and devices a box may contain, based on its volume.
The top of the final flooring, the reference for box, counter and fixture heights. AFF means above finished floor.
Non-metallic sheathed copper cable used for most house wiring in Canada (often called by a brand name).
Steel plate nailed over the face of a stud or joist to protect a cable or pipe that is too close to the edge.
Insulated staple that secures cable to framing without damaging the sheath.
A recessed light fixture approved for direct contact with insulation; IC/AT also means airtight.
Ground-fault circuit interrupter - trips when current leaks to ground, used near water.
Arc-fault circuit interrupter - trips on dangerous arcing in wiring; required on most dwelling branch circuits.
Parking with an energized outlet (or load-managed circuit) ready for an electric vehicle charger, required by many BC municipalities.
The wiring from the panel breaker to the outlets it serves.
Drain, waste and vent - the gravity piping that carries sewage out and lets air in to protect traps.
A U-shaped fitting that holds water to block sewer gas; every fixture needs one.
The pipe from a trap to its vent; limited in length so the trap is not siphoned.
Vertical vent pipe that goes through the roof and lets air into the drain system.
A vertical drain or vent pipe running through one or more storeys.
An access fitting with a removable plug for rodding a drain.
The lowest horizontal drain inside the building that collects all the stacks and runs to the building sewer.
The fall of a horizontal drain, expressed as a ratio (1 in 50) or per cent (2%) or inches per foot (1/4 in).
The fitting at the floor that connects a toilet to the drain; normally 305 mm (12 in) from the finished wall.
Cross-linked polyethylene tubing used for water supply; flexible, joined with crimp, clamp or expansion fittings.
A distribution header that feeds individual fixture lines, often with a shut-off per line.
Pressure-reducing valve that lowers street water pressure to a safe level for the house.
A device that stops water flowing back from the house into the public supply.
A valve that blends hot and cold water to limit the outlet temperature and prevent scalding.
A valve that isolates a fixture, a zone or the whole house.
Filling DWV piping with water (to a set head) to check for leaks before cover-up.
Pressurizing piping with air and watching a gauge to check for leaks.
CSA F280, the standard for room-by-room heat loss and gain used to size heating and cooling equipment in houses.
The rate a house loses heat at the design outdoor temperature, in watts; sets the heating capacity.
The cold (and hot) outdoor temperatures the system is sized for, listed for each location in the code's climatic data.
Equipment that moves heat from outdoor air (or ground) into the house in winter and out in summer; the usual low-carbon choice in BC.
The main supply or return duct from the air handler that branches feed off.
Heat recovery ventilator - balanced fans that exchange stale indoor air for fresh outdoor air and recover most of the heat.
Energy recovery ventilator - like an HRV but also transfers some moisture.
The main continuously-capable exhaust fan of a house ventilation system, sized by the code.
Ventilation that supplies about as much air as it exhausts, as an HRV does.
A fan that removes air from a kitchen, bathroom or laundry to the outdoors.
A flap in an exhaust duct or hood that closes when the fan is off.
A joist bay closed with sheet metal and used as a return-air duct; must be sealed.
The duct fitting that transitions from a round branch to the rectangular floor or wall register.
Marking of buried utilities on the ground (paint and flags) by the utility owners after a BC 1 Call request.
The strip either side of a locate mark inside which you must hand-dig or hydro-vac, not machine dig.
Excavation with pressurised water and a vacuum truck, used to expose utilities safely.
Horizontal boards on stakes set outside the excavation that hold string lines marking the foundation.
A fixed point of known elevation used to set every height on the job.
The minimum distance from a property line to the building, set by the municipal zoning bylaw.
A surveyor's check of the foundation forms or footings against the setbacks and elevations, often required by BC municipalities before the pour.
Height relative to the national vertical datum (sea level), used on surveys and in the HASWORKS HOMES Site view.
Natural soil that has not been dug or loosened; footings must bear on it, rock or compacted fill.
How deep the ground freezes. Footings in frost-susceptible soils go below it so frost heave cannot lift them.
Digging deeper than the footing elevation. The extra depth must be filled with compacted granular or concrete, not loose soil.
The pressure the soil can carry without excessive settlement. Part 9 footing tables assume a minimum; poor soils need an engineer.
Soil placed back against the foundation after it is built, dampproofed and drained.
The ground surface around the building; finished grade is the final landscaped level. 'Grading' is shaping it to drain.
An excavated, lined pit outside a below-grade window that lets light in and must drain.
A drain inlet with a sump that collects surface water, e.g. at the bottom of a driveway sloping toward a garage.
The vertical pipe that carries water from the eavestrough to the ground or a storm connection.
The widened concrete base under a foundation wall or post that spreads load onto the soil.
A footing that changes level in steps on a sloping site; each step may rise at most 600 mm.
A groove formed in the top of a footing so the wall concrete locks into it.
Steel reinforcing bar placed in concrete to carry tension. Size and spacing come from the code or the engineer.
Temporary panels, ties and bracing that hold wet concrete in shape.
The concrete, ICF or block wall from the footing up to the floor framing that resists soil pressure.
Insulating concrete form - hollow foam blocks stacked and filled with concrete, leaving insulation on both faces.
Metal tie holding the two sides of wall forms apart; snapped off after stripping and the holes sealed.
A planned weakened line in a slab or wall so shrinkage cracks happen there, neatly.
A bolt cast into the foundation that fastens the sill plate - at least 12.7 mm diameter, no more than 2.4 m apart.
A short pipe cast into concrete so a service can pass through later without coring.
A coating on the outside of the foundation below grade that resists moisture moving through by capillarity.
A membrane system that keeps out water under hydrostatic pressure; more than dampproofing.
A dimpled plastic sheet against the foundation that creates a drainage gap down to the footing drain.
Pressure from standing groundwater pushing on walls and slabs.
Perforated pipe around the footing in clean stone that collects groundwater.
A pit that collects drain water, with a pump where it cannot drain by gravity.
An underground pit filled with stone that lets drain water soak into the ground, where allowed.
Geotextile wrapped around drain stone or pipe that keeps soil fines out.
A colourless radioactive gas from uranium in soil; Health Canada's guideline is 200 Bq/m3.
Gases from the ground (radon, methane, moisture) that can enter through slabs and walls.
A radon fan pulling air from the gravel under the slab and exhausting it outside, keeping soil gas out.
The layer under the slab (100 mm clean granular or equivalent) through which soil gas can be drawn to the radon pipe.
Plastic sheet (usually 0.15 mm / 6 mil) used as soil-gas barrier, ground cover, and interior air and vapour barrier.
The code term for a concrete slab placed on the ground.
A sheet or layer between the slab and footing or rock so they can move separately.
The treated wood plate on top of the foundation that the floor framing sits on.
Foam or EPDM strip under the sill plate that seals the gap to the concrete and acts as a capillary break.
A shallow space under the floor, either heated (inside the envelope) or unheated (vented to outside).
The membrane laid on the soil of a crawl space to stop moisture and soil gas.
